record.original_question: What additional invariants, recognition methods, or classification principles can distinguish the Kishino virtual knot from the unknot and clarify when a non-trivial virtual knot can arise as the connected sum of two trivial virtual knots, especially in view of the fact that connected sum is not well defined for closed virtual knots but is ordered and well defined for long virtual knots?

evidence.quote: Are we done with this knot? Perhaps not. Other proofs of its non-triviality may be illuminating. The fact that the Kishino diagram is non-trivial and yet a connected sum of trivial virtual knots suggests the question: Classify when a non-trivial virtual knot can be the connected sum of two trivial virtual knots.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background. A virtual knot diagram is a 4-valent planar graph whose vertices are decorated either as classical crossings (over/under information) or as virtual crossings (drawn with a small circle), considered up to the generalized Reidemeister moves (the three classical Reidemeister moves together with the four virtual Reidemeister moves and the mixed move). A virtual knot is an equivalence class of such diagrams. A long virtual knot is an equivalence class of virtual tangle diagrams with two free ends going off to infinity (a 1–1 tangle), considered up to the same moves; for long virtual knots the connected sum operation, defined by concatenating one tangle to the other, is well defined and noncommutative (ordered). For closed virtual knots the connected sum is in general not well defined, since the result can depend on the chosen base points and the diagrams used.

The Kishino diagram is a specific virtual knot diagram which is presented as the connected sum of two diagrams each of which represents the trivial (closed) virtual knot, and which is itself nontrivial as a virtual knot.

Problem. Give a complete classification of those nontrivial closed virtual knots K which can be represented as a connected sum K = K_1 # K_2 of two trivial virtual knots K_1 and K_2 (for some choice of diagrams and base points realizing this connected sum). Equivalently, characterize intrinsically (e.g. by an invariant or a structural criterion) the closed virtual knots that arise in this way, and provide invariants or recognition methods that distinguish such connected sums (in particular, the Kishino virtual knot) from the unknot.
artifact.status_search_result: The Kishino knot itself has been proven nontrivial by many invariants (3-strand Jones polynomial, surface bracket of Dye–Kauffman, Manturov's Ξ-polynomial, quaternionic biquandle of Fenn–Bartholomew, etc.), and it is known that if a connected sum K_1#K_2 of virtual knots is trivial then both factors are trivial. However, a complete classification of which nontrivial closed virtual knots arise as connected sums of two trivial virtual knots does not appear in the literature; surveys of unsolved problems in virtual knot theory continue to list questions in this circle.

status_evidence.title: Virtual Knot Theory – Unsolved Problems
status_evidence.snippet: Connected sum of virtual knots is not well-defined; the Kishino knot is the standard example of a nontrivial virtual knot that is a connected sum of two trivial diagrams.
status_evidence.claim: Problem listed among unsolved problems in virtual knot theory.

status_evidence.title: Compact and long virtual knots
status_evidence.snippet: If K1#K2 is trivial then both K1 and K2 are trivial; connected sum is well-defined for long virtual knots but not for closed virtual knots.
status_evidence.claim: Partial structural results known about connected sums of virtual knots.

status_evidence.title: Introduction to Virtual Knot Theory
status_evidence.snippet: The Kishino diagram is shown nontrivial by multiple invariants, but full classification of trivial-#-trivial nontrivial connected sums is not given.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple invariants detect Kishino but classification question remains.
